newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Europe ministers see need to harmonize taxes.
newsitem.headline: Europe ministers see need to harmonize taxes.

text.p: Taxes will follow jobs as the next big area for European policy coordination on the route to currency union, finance ministers said on Monday, but the road ahead is far from clear.

A working group of EU officials has been discussing coordination of tax policies since the start of the year without significant results, and the issue is due to be discussed at an informal meeting of finance ministers in September.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel and his colleagues in higher-tax countries are concerned that some neighbouring states are luring away capital investment and the jobs that go with them by offering more favourable corporate tax rates.
Competition for scarce jobs lies at the heart of potential conflicts among the European allies.
Waigel said at the start of an EU finance ministers' meeting that Bonn felt a strong need for coordination of tax policies to eliminate unfair competition.
"We want to have a fairness code on direct taxes to prevent competition," he told the finance ministers in an open discussion.

But his French counterpart Dominique Strauss-Kahn, who recently won commitments for more forceful action on jobs, said a code of conduct as proposed by Waigel would not be enough, that binding rules would be necessary.
Italian Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi urged that the Luxembourg EU presidency now starting continue efforts towards tax harmonisation, including taxation of the financial markets sector.
Waigel has prepared a tax reform package that would cut German corporate taxes to levels he says would be competitive while broadening the tax base.
But after passing the lower house of the German parliament, it was voted down last week by the opposition-dominated upper house and is now languishing in an uncertain mediation process.
Waigel said intensive discussions are needed on coordination of economic policies, leading to final approval of the resolutions jointly adopted at last month's Amsterdam summit.
On indirect taxes, he said he hoped Europe would adopt a "nation-of-origin" system, under which the taxes would be paid in the country that produced the goods rather than where they are sold.
Strauss-Kahn said he wanted to take the Waigel proposal of a codex a step further. "We have to go beyond a code of tax conduct, we need concrete measures," he told the same meeting.
Ciampi said, "During the Luxembourg presidency, we must continue the process of tax harmonisation in all sectors, including the financial markets sector."
He added that the last leg towards European monetary union (EMU) would require governments to manage and implement the principles of the EMU stability pact.
The single currency would mean losing all flexibility over exchange rate policy making it necessary to increase flexibility in all other areas, including capital and labour, he added.
